subject: Justin Martyr (St Justin the Philosopher)
texts_on_disk: design/saints-hub/sources/people/justin-martyr/ (gitignored). raw/ holds whole CCEL volumes (anf01.txt, anf02.txt, anf03.txt, anf06.txt, npnf201.txt, npnf203.txt) and the fetched web pages; the named .txt files are the works or chapters cut from them, or stripped web pages (first line names the URL where it is an excerpt). Every 'exact' below was searched by script (scratchpad justin/chk.py: footnote marks like [1783] removed, whitespace, dashes and curly quotes folded, case ignored) in the file named in 'evidence_file', and for Justin's own works the chapter heading above the match was read back and compared with 'place'. The 'check' block records the result. For Justin's works each line was also searched in New Advent's revised copy ('newadvent_revised').

text_used.text: Justin's works are quoted from the translation of Marcus Dods and George Reith in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1 (1885), as printed on CCEL (plain text marked 'Rights: Public Domain'). The Martyrdom is Marcus Dods's translation in the same volume. Other writers: Tatian (J. E. Ryland, ANF 2), Irenaeus (Roberts and Rambaut, ANF 1), Tertullian (ANF 3), Methodius (W. R. Clark, ANF 6), Eusebius (A. C. McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890). 'exact' is the text as printed with footnote numbers taken out. 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God.
text_used.source: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL plain text
text_used.note: New Advent prints a revised copy of the same translation (Kevin Knight). It differs in small ways: 'whilst' becomes 'while', 'expected forthwith' becomes 'expected immediately', and Dialogue chapter 1 has '(In jest.)' where CCEL reads 'So I replied to him in jest.' Every line below is in the CCEL form; where New Advent differs, the note says so. CCEL chapter pages follow the pattern anf01.viii.ii.<chapter> (First Apology), viii.iii (Second Apology), viii.iv (Dialogue), viii.xi (Martyrdom). ANF numbers the chapters of the Second Apology in the traditional order; some modern editions renumber it.

born.text: Born about 100 at Flavia Neapolis in Palestine, today Nablus. Estimates run from about 100 to about 114.
born.source: First Apology, chapter 1 ('I, Justin, the son of Priscus and grandson of Bacchius, natives of Flavia Neapolis in Palestine'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'born at Flavia Neapolis, about A.D. 100'; Britannica: 'born c. 100, Flavia Neapolis, Palestine [now Nāblus]'; Merriam-Webster: 'circa 100– circa 165'
born.note: Other dates: Dods and Reith's ANF note says 'about a.d. 114'; OCA 'around 114'; the Episcopal Church (LFF 2022) 'about the year 110'; the Greek Great Synaxaristes 110. His own words fix only the town. Flavia Neapolis was founded by Vespasian near ancient Shechem (Catholic Encyclopedia); OCA's 'Sychem' is the old town nearby. Plain wording that holds: 'About 100. Some say as late as 114.'

evidence.exact: I, Justin, the son of Priscus and grandson of Bacchius, natives of Flavia Neapolis in Palestine
evidence.display: I, Justin, the son of Priscus and grandson of Bacchius, natives of Flavia Neapolis in Palestine
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

grew_up.text: In a pagan family. His grandfather's name is Greek, his father's and his own Latin. He calls himself uncircumcised, and speaks of the Samaritans as his own people, though he was not a Samaritan by religion. He studied Greek philosophy before he met the Scriptures.
grew_up.source: First Apology 1; Dialogue 28 ('although I am an uncircumcised man'); Dialogue 120 ('any of my people, that is, the Samaritans'); Wace, Dictionary of Christian Biography (1911), 'Justinus Martyr' ('The name of his grandfather is Greek; of his father and himself Latin'; 'obviously not a Samaritan by blood or religion'); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910)

evidence.exact: although I am an uncircumcised man
evidence.display: although I am an uncircumcised man
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

evidence.exact: For I gave no thought to any of my people, that is, the Samaritans
evidence.display: For I gave no thought to any of my people, that is, the Samaritans
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

died.text: About 165, at Rome. He was scourged and beheaded with six companions, on the sentence of Rusticus, prefect of the city, after they refused to sacrifice to the gods.
died.source: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapters 1 and 5; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'condemned to death by the prefect, Rusticus, towards A.D. 165, with six companions'; Dods and Reith (ANF 1): 'The Chronicon Paschale gives as the date 165 a.d.'; McGiffert (NPNF2-1, Eusebius 4.16 note): Rusticus 'became prefect of Rome in 163'
died.note: No ancient text gives the day. Rusticus's term (from 162 or 163 to about 168) brackets the year. The Episcopal Church prints 167; the Church of England and the ELCA print c. 165. Eusebius dates it under Marcus Aurelius (4.16).

evidence.exact: Let those who have refused to sacrifice to the gods and to yield to the command of the emperor be scourged, and led away to suffer the punishment of decapitation, according to the laws.
evidence.display: Let those who have refused to sacrifice to the gods and to yield to the command of the emperor be scourged, and led away to suffer the punishment of decapitation, according to the laws.
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

buried.text: The record of his trial does not say. It says only that some believers secretly took the bodies and laid them 'in a suitable place'. The OCA says his relics rest in Rome.
buried.note: Later claims: OCA says 'The relics of Saint Justin the Philosopher rest in Rome'; the church of St John the Baptist at Sacrofano, north of Rome, claims his bones (Wikipedia, citing the church). Treat both as later tradition. Bones kept at Annapolis, Maryland, once linked to him, are now said to be of a third-century Justin (Wikipedia).

evidence.exact: And some of the faithful having secretly removed their bodies, laid them in a suitable place
evidence.display: And some of the faithful having secretly removed their bodies, laid them in a suitable place
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

buried.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: 'Nobody knows where' went beyond the source (the Martyrdom is silent; OCA and Sacrofano claim relics). Now states what the record says and gives the OCA's claim as the OCA's.

also_called.text: Justin the Philosopher: OCA 'Martyr Justin the Philosopher and those with him at Rome'; Russian 'Мученик Иустин Философ, Великий, Римский' (Martyr Justin the Philosopher, the Great, of Rome).
Justin the Apologist and Philosopher (Greek 'Άγιος Ιουστίνος ο Απολογητής και φιλόσοφος'); the Great Synaxaristes has 'Ὁ Ἅγιος Ἰουστίνος ὁ Μάρτυρας ὁ Φιλόσοφος'.
Saint Justin, Martyr (Catholic calendar). 'Martyr' is a title, not a surname.
also_called.note: The oldest use of the double title: Tertullian, about 207, 'Justin, philosopher and martyr' (Against the Valentinians, chapter 5).

status.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans (Church of England Lesser Festival, printed in roman type, not italics; Episcopal Church). Lutherans (LCMS, ELCA) remember him, all on 1 June.
status.source: USCCB 2026 calendar (Memorial); OCA; saint.gr; Church of England Common Worship calendar; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; CPH (LCMS) commemorations; Evangelical Lutheran Worship church year
status.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the page's status line said Anglicans 'remember' him while its church table says Anglican 'Saint' (the Martin form). Made consistent with Martin's page.

patron_of.text: Philosophers, in Catholic devotion (Franciscan Media). The OCA says he is invoked by those who seek help in their studies.
patron_of.source: Franciscan Media, Saint of the Day ('As patron of philosophers, Saint Justin Martyr...'); OCA ('He is invoked by those who seek help in their studies', of the Russian Church)
patron_of.note: No ancient source gives a patronage. Wikipedia's infobox also says 'Philosophers', citing Catholic News Agency (2011). Nothing else found with a source.
patron_of.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the OCA sentence follows one about the Russian Church but does not itself limit the invoking to it; the page now attributes it to the OCA.

in_art.text: In Eastern icons, such as the Stavronikita fresco: a dark-haired, bearded man in a cloak, with a small cross and a book; the fresco labels him 'the Philosopher'. A Western print of 1584 (Thevet) imagines an old man with a long beard.
in_art.source: The pictures themselves: Theophanes the Cretan's fresco at Stavronikita (labelled Ο ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΟΣ, cross in his right hand, book in his left); the Recklinghausen Menaion icon (cross); André Thevet, Les vrais pourtraits (1584)
in_art.note: Described from the images, not from an iconography handbook. No attribute list for Justin was found in a reference work.
in_art.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: 'often labelled' and 'prints of the 1500s' generalised from two pictures; narrowed to the pictures actually seen.

wrote.text: Three works survive that are surely his: the First Apology, the Second Apology and the Dialogue with Trypho. Eusebius lists more that are lost. Several works printed under his name are not his.
wrote.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'There are extant but three works of Justin, of which the authenticity is assured: the two "Apologies" and the "Dialogue"'; Eusebius, Church History 4.18; Dods and Reith, ANF 1 introductory note (three classes of works); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('Three of his works survive'); Britannica
wrote.note: Eusebius's list of lost works: a Discourse to the Greeks, a Refutation, On the Sovereignty of God, the Psaltes, On the Soul, a work against Marcion (4.11, 4.18), and his own 'work against all the heresies' (First Apology 26).

pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster's biographical entry reads 'Jus·tin ˈjə-stən ... Saint circa 100– circa 165 Justin (the) Martyr church father'.

roles.text: Philosopher: tried four schools of philosophy, and kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after he became a Christian.
roles.source: Dialogue 1-2 and 8; Eusebius 4.11 ('In the guise of a philosopher he preached the divine word')

roles.text: Teacher: taught in Rome from rooms 'above one Martinus', and anyone who came to him heard 'the doctrines of truth'.
roles.note: Vatican News and Britannica say he opened a school; the Martyrdom only says whoever came to him was taught.

roles.text: Apologist: wrote defences of the Christians to the emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons, and to the Roman Senate.
roles.source: First Apology 1; Second Apology title; Eusebius 4.18

roles.text: Martyr: beheaded at Rome about 165 with six companions.
roles.source: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapters 3 and 5

west.source: USCCB, Liturgical Calendar for the Dioceses of the United States 2026: '1 Mon Saint Justin, Martyr ... red ... Memorial'
west.note: bible.usccb.org day pages answered 403 (bot check); the USCCB's own 2026 calendar PDF was read instead.

west.text: 13 April in the 1916 Roman Martyrology ('there suffered at Rome that remarkable man, Justin the Philosopher'), with his feast on 14 April ('feast of St. Justin, martyr, who is mentioned on the 13th of this month').
west.note: Text on disk: sources/people/justin-martyr/martyrology-1916-april-13-14.txt. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'Leo XIII had a Mass and an Office composed in his honour and set his feast for 14 April.' Catholic Culture: in the 1962 Missal 'St. Justin's feast was celebrated on April 14.'

west.text: 1 June, Lesser Festival: 'Justin, Martyr at Rome, c.165'.
west.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (roman type = Lesser Festival; italics = Commemoration)
The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022
Concordia Publishing House (LCMS), 'Complete List of Church Year Commemorations' (Lutheran Service Book)
Evangelical Lutheran Worship, The Church Year (final draft, January 2006, ELCA)
west.note: The same document used for Martin. Seen in the ELW draft, not in a current ELCA web page.

east.text: 1 June: 'Martyr Justin the Philosopher and those with him at Rome'.
1 June: 'Εορτάζει στις 1 Ιουνίου εκάστου έτους' (saint.gr); 'Ημ. Εορτής: 1 Ιουνίου' (Great Synaxaristes).
east.note: GOARCH answered 403 (bot check) and was not read.

east.text: 1 June on the old calendar, which is 14 June on today's calendar: 'День памяти 14 июня'.

note.text: East and West now share 1 June. The Roman calendar kept 14 April from 1882. The 1969 calendar moved him to 1 June, because 14 April often fell among the Easter feasts and the Byzantines had kept 1 June since at least the 9th century.
note.source: Calendarium Romanum (Typis Polyglottis Vaticanis, 1969), pp. 94 and 120; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), 'St. Justin Martyr'; Catholic Culture (1962 Missal: April 14); USCCB 2026
note.note: Checked 2026-09-25 in the Calendarium Romanum itself (editio typica, Typis Polyglottis Vaticanis, MCMLXIX; archive.org OCR, excerpt in calendarium-romanum-1969-justin.txt). Page 94, under IUNIUS 1: 'Eius festum ascriptum est in Calendario romano anno 1882, die 14 aprilis celebrandum, postridie memoriam eius in Martyrologio Flori. Cum tamen dies ista saepius in sollemnitates paschales incidat, memoria S. Iustini in diem 1 iunii translata est, qua die agitur apud Byzantinos, saltem a saeculo ix.' Page 120, under April 14: 'Memoria S. Iustini, dum eius natalis dies ignoretur, die 1 iunii reponitur, qua die apud Byzantinos colitur.' The June table lists '1 S. Iustini, martyris Memoria'. The page says this in our own words (no quotation). Churches on the old calendar keep 1 June 13 days later, on 14 June.

numbers.text: 4 schools of philosophy before Christ: a Stoic, a Peripatetic, a Pythagorean and the Platonists.
numbers.note: The Stoic 'did not know himself'; the Peripatetic asked for his fee after a few days; the Pythagorean sent him away for not knowing music, astronomy and geometry.

evidence.exact: this man, after having entertained me for the first few days, requested me to settle the fee
evidence.display: this man, after having entertained me for the first few days, requested me to settle the fee
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

numbers.text: 3 works survive that are surely his.
1 manuscript: all three works come down to us through a single medieval manuscript, Paris gr. 450, finished on 11 September 1364. The only other copy was made from it.
numbers.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'Paris gr. 450, finished on 11 September, 1364; and Claromont. 82, written in 1571 ... The second is only a copy of the first, which is therefore our sole authority'
numbers.note: Wikipedia adds that it was bought in Venice about 1540 and first printed by Robert Estienne in 1551 (not checked further). The Catholic Encyclopedia says the manuscript has 'many large gaps'.

numbers.text: 2 days of debate with Trypho: the Dialogue speaks of those who came 'on the second day'.
numbers.source: Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 85 and 142; Eusebius 4.18 (at Ephesus)
numbers.note: The Dialogue never says 'two days' in so many words; it refers to 'yesterday' and to those who came 'on the second day', and ends on that day.

evidence.exact: Then one of those who had come with them on the second day
evidence.display: Then one of those who had come with them on the second day
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain
evidence.note: New Advent's revised copy words this differently; print the CCEL (1885) form.

numbers.text: 6 companions died with him: Chariton, Charito (a woman), Euelpistus (a servant of Caesar), Hierax, Paeon and Liberianus.
numbers.source: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapter 3; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) ('six companions')
numbers.note: OCA's list differs (it adds Valerian and Justus); the three versions of the Acts do not agree on every name.
lines: Only one says Justin taught him

numbers.text: 150 years: he writes that Christ was born 'one hundred and fifty years ago', which dates the First Apology to about 150.
numbers.source: First Apology, chapter 46; Wace (1911): 'the year 148—i.e. Justin's A.D. 150—should be taken as the approximate date'
numbers.note: A round number in his own words. Britannica: 'addressed about 150'.

evidence.exact: Christ was born one hundred and fifty years ago under Cyrenius
evidence.display: Christ was born one hundred and fifty years ago under Cyrenius
evidence.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

traits.text: Restless and impatient. When the Pythagorean told him to learn music, astronomy and geometry first, he could not face the wait.
traits.title: a restless seeker

quote.exact: Accordingly I took it rather impatiently
quote.display: Accordingly I took it rather impatiently
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

quote2.exact: I was not able to endure longer procrastination.
quote2.display: I was not able to endure longer procrastination.
quote2.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

traits.text: Good-humoured and courteous in argument. He answered Trypho's greeting with a line of Homer, 'in jest'. Two days later they parted as friends, and he left praying for them.
traits.source: Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 1 and 142 (ANF footnote: the reply quotes Homer, Iliad 6.123)
traits.note: New Advent prints '(In jest.)' as a stage note; CCEL's 1885 text reads 'So I replied to him in jest.'
traits.title: joked, and parted friends

quote.exact: "But who are you, most excellent man?" So I replied to him in jest.
quote.display: "But who are you, most excellent man?" So I replied to him in jest.
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain
quote.note: New Advent's revised copy words this differently; print the CCEL (1885) form.

quote2.exact: And I, praying for them, said
quote2.display: And I, praying for them, said
quote2.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

traits.text: Would not pretend. Pressed on whether he really believed in a rebuilt Jerusalem, he said so plainly, and admitted many good Christians disagreed with him. He wrote that Christians could deny their faith and live, but would not live by a lie.
traits.title: no double talk

quote.exact: I am not so miserable a fellow, Trypho, as to say one thing and think another.
quote.display: I am not so miserable a fellow, Trypho, as to say one thing and think another.
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

quote2.exact: for it is in our power, when we are examined, to deny that we are Christians; but we would not live by telling a lie.
quote2.display: for it is in our power, when we are examined, to deny that we are Christians; but we would not live by telling a lie.
quote2.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

traits.text: Bold in public debate. He cross-examined the Cynic Crescens in public and offered to do it again before the emperor. When Trypho's friends jeered, he got up to leave.
traits.title: took on all comers

quote.exact: I proposed to him certain questions on this subject, and interrogated him, and found most convincingly that he, in truth, knows nothing.
quote.display: I proposed to him certain questions on this subject, and interrogated him, and found most convincingly that he, in truth, knows nothing.
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

quote2.exact: Then I rose up and was about to leave
quote2.display: Then I rose up and was about to leave
quote2.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

lede.text: Nearly everything about his life comes from his own books and the short record of his trial. A few men who knew him or read him soon after left a line.
lede.source: Wace (1911): 'What we know of him is gathered almost entirely from his own writings'

quotes.exact: And the most admirable Justin has rightly denounced them as robbers.
quotes.display: And the most admirable Justin has rightly denounced them as robbers.
quotes.note: Tatian was 'a hearer of Justin's' (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.28.1). In chapter 19 he says Crescens tried to have Justin, 'and indeed me', put to death. Also on New Advent 0202 (same wording).

quotes.exact: for instance Justin, philosopher and martyr;
quotes.note: The earliest writer to give him both titles. Tertullian names him first among those who had already refuted the heretics. (Tertullian is not himself counted a saint.)
quotes.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: 'the earliest writer to give him both titles' and 'about 207' had no source on disk; replaced with what the text itself shows (he names Justin first among those who refuted the heresy).

quotes.exact: Now Justin of Neapolis, a man not far removed either from the times or from the virtues of the apostles
quotes.display: Justin of Neapolis, a man not far removed either from the times or from the virtues of the apostles
quotes.work: Methodius, From the Discourse on the Resurrection, Part III
quotes.note: Also on New Advent (fathers/0625.htm), same wording; that page is the link. Methodius wrote about a century and a half after Justin, so this is reputation, not memory.

quotes.exact: But Justin was especially prominent in those days. In the guise of a philosopher he preached the divine word, and contended for the faith in his writings.
quotes.display: But Justin was especially prominent in those days. In the guise of a philosopher he preached the divine word, and contended for the faith in his writings.
quotes.translation: A. C. McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1 (1890)
quotes.note: Also 4.8: 'Justin, a genuine lover of the true philosophy'.

life_moments.text: Born to a pagan family in Flavia Neapolis, a Roman town in Samaria built near ancient Shechem. He names his father and grandfather in the first line of his First Apology.
life_moments.title: A Gentile in Samaria

life_moments.text: He went looking for God in the schools. A Stoic taught him nothing about God. A Peripatetic asked for his fee after a few days, so Justin decided he was no philosopher. A proud Pythagorean sent him away for not knowing geometry. The Platonists thrilled him, and he thought he would soon see God.
life_moments.note: The Catholic Encyclopedia warns the story is shaped to make a point: 'This account cannot be taken too literally.'
life_moments.title: Shopping for a philosophy

quote.exact: and such was my stupidity, I expected forthwith to look upon God, for this is the end of Plato's philosophy.
quote.display: and such was my stupidity, I expected forthwith to look upon God, for this is the end of Plato's philosophy.
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain
quote.note: New Advent's revised copy words this differently; print the CCEL (1885) form.

life_moments.text: He liked to walk alone to think, in a field near the sea. An old man followed him there and took his Platonism apart, question by question. He sent Justin to the prophets, and Justin never saw him again. Watching Christians face death without fear had already shaken him.
life_moments.source: Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 3 to 8; Second Apology, chapter 12
life_moments.note: He does not name the place. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it the seashore; Eusebius's 'Ephesus' belongs to the Trypho debate, not to this walk.
life_moments.title: The old man

quote.exact: When he had spoken these and many other things, which there is no time for mentioning at present, he went away, bidding me attend to them; and I have not seen him since.
quote.display: When he had spoken these and many other things, which there is no time for mentioning at present, he went away, bidding me attend to them; and I have not seen him since.
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

quote2.exact: and heard the Christians slandered, and saw them fearless of death
quote2.display: and heard the Christians slandered, and saw them fearless of death
quote2.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

life_moments.text: One morning a Jew named Trypho, who had fled the war in Judea, greeted him in a colonnade because of his philosopher's cloak. When Trypho's friends jeered, Justin got up to go, but Trypho held him by the cloak. They argued over the Scriptures for two days and parted friends.
life_moments.source: Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 1, 9 and 142; Eusebius, Church History 4.18 (at Ephesus)
life_moments.note: The war is the Bar Kokhba revolt (ANF footnote), 132 to 135.
life_moments.title: Two days with Trypho

quote.exact: remember us as friends when you are gone
quote.display: remember us as friends when you are gone
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

life_moments.text: He wrote to the emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons for 'those of all nations who are unjustly hated'. He asked that Christians be judged by what they did, not by their name. He also described how Christians met on Sunday, read the Gospels and the prophets, prayed and shared the bread and cup.
life_moments.note: Britannica: 'addressed about 150'. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls his account of the Mass 'a richness of detail unique for that age'.
life_moments.title: A letter to the emperor

quote.exact: present this address and petition in behalf of those of all nations who are unjustly hated and wantonly abused, myself being one of them.
quote.display: present this address and petition in behalf of those of all nations who are unjustly hated and wantonly abused, myself being one of them.
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain
quote.note: New Advent's revised copy words this differently; print the CCEL (1885) form.

life_moments.text: After the prefect Urbicus had a Christian teacher, Ptolemaeus, and two others put to death for the name alone, Justin wrote again. He said he expected the Cynic Crescens, whom he had beaten in public debate, to plot his death.
life_moments.title: He saw it coming

quote.exact: I too, therefore, expect to be plotted against and fixed to the stake, by some of those I have named, or perhaps by Crescens, that lover of bravado and boasting
quote.display: I too, therefore, expect to be plotted against and fixed to the stake, by some of those I have named, or perhaps by Crescens, that lover of bravado and boasting
quote.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), CCEL, public domain

life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the Catholic Encyclopedia says the Second Apology 'must have been written shortly afterwards'; 'A few years later' had no source. Also: Justin writes 'by some of those I have named, or perhaps by Crescens', so the page no longer says he expected Crescens; and the text addresses 'Romans' (the title 'to the Roman Senate' is the edition's).

life_moments.text: He and six others were brought before Rusticus, prefect of Rome. Justin gave his address, above one Martinus by the Timiotinian Bath, and said it was his second time living in Rome. All refused to sacrifice. They were scourged and beheaded.
life_moments.source: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapters 1 to 5
life_moments.title: Before the prefect

quote.exact: I live above one Martinus, at the Timiotinian Bath; and during the whole time (and I am now living in Rome for the second time) I am unaware of any other meeting than his.
quote.display: I live above one Martinus, at the Timiotinian Bath; and during the whole time (and I am now living in Rome for the second time) I am unaware of any other meeting than his.

miracles.text: None recorded. The Martyrdom, Tatian, Irenaeus, Eusebius and Jerome tell no wonders worked by Justin or at his death. Leave the miracles section out of his page.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: Justin said 'plain singing' without 'lifeless organs, with dancing, and cymbals' is the Church's way. Truth: the line comes from the Answers to the Orthodox, a later work printed under his name. Dods and Reith put the 'Replies to the Orthodox' among works 'unquestionably not the works of Justin', and say they were written after the Council of Nicaea (325).

misquoted_or_legend.note: Checked 2026-09-25. Greek: Migne PG 6 (archive.org OCR, excerpt in migne-pg6-quaestiones-ad-orthodoxos-107.txt), under the running head QUAESTIONES ET RESPONSIONES AD ORTHODOXOS, col. 1355: question headed 'ΕΡΩΤΗΣΙΣ ΡΖʹ' (107), answer 'Οὐ τὸ ᾆσαι ἁπλῶς ἐστι τοῖς νηπίοις ἁρμόδιον, ἀλλὰ τὸ μετὰ τῶν ἀψύχων ὀργάνων ᾆσαι, καὶ μετὰ ὀρχήσεως καὶ κροτάλων' (normalised here; the OCR has minor letter errors). hard_topics.text: The Jews in the Dialogue. The debate is courteous and ends in friendship, but Justin says the Jews' sufferings after the war came 'in fairness and justice', because they killed Christ and curse Christians in their synagogues. Britannica sums up his claim that 'the gentiles have been chosen to replace Israel as God's chosen people'. Ben Zion Bokser (Encyclopaedia Judaica) writes that Justin's 'invective against Jews and Judaism entered the mainstream of Christian thought and became a sinister influence', contributing to Christian antisemitism.

hard_topics.text: The Son 'in the second place'. Justin calls Christ God, but also 'another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things', and puts Him 'in the second place'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) speaks of 'the subordinationism of Justin's theology', from 'philosophic speculation', while crediting him with the Word's 'Divinity and Incarnation'. He wrote long before the Council of Nicaea (325).

hub_card.note: Groups and 'pre300' are right (born about 100, died about 165). Not 'teachers' (that collection is the Doctors). Side: the hint said 'east'; I suggest both. He was born in Samaria and wrote in Greek, but he lived in Rome twice, taught there, wrote to the emperor there and died there, and Rome's calendar and the Byzantine calendar both keep him on 1 June. If the filter means 'which half of the Church claims him', both do; if it means 'where he wrote', east. Owner's call.

site_data_flags.text: people.justin.who: 'Philosopher who became the first great defender of the faith.' 'First great' holds; avoid 'the first apologist'. Dods and Reith: 'He was not the first that wrote an Apology in behalf of the Christians, but his Apologies are the earliest extant' (1885), and Aristides' Apology, found later, may be older.
site_data_flags.note: The Aristides point is from general knowledge; not checked here.

site_data_flags.text: people.justin.hook: 'A stranger by the sea talked him into Christ.' Justin says 'a certain field not far from the sea'. Fair as plain words.

items.text: Two puns, both pointed out in the translators' notes: Christos and chrestos ("we are most excellent people"), and Crescens as "that lover of bravado and boasting" (Greek philopsophou kai philokompou, sounding like philosopher).
items.source: First Apology 4 with note 1772; Second Apology 3 with note 1930

items.text: The old man said he had come looking for some of his household who had gone away from him.
Urbicus had Ptolemaeus put to death; Lucius protested and was led away too; then a third man. The Second Apology is titled as addressed to the Roman Senate.
Brief and concise utterances fell from Him, for He was no sophist, but His word was the power of God.
Baptism after prayer and fasting, with the church fasting too; washing in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
The kiss, bread and a cup of wine mixed with water brought to the one presiding, thanks at length, Amen, deacons carry portions to the absent.

Only the baptised who live as Christ enjoined may receive the Eucharist; the translators' note 1911: the passage is claimed alike by Calvinists, Lutherans, and Romanists (Coxe's bracketed addition dissents from calling it inexact).

Sunday: readings, the president's instruction, all rise to pray, the bread and cup, a collection from those well to do and willing for orphans, widows, the sick, those in bonds and strangers; Sunday because it is the first day of creation and the day of the resurrection.
The fuller First Apology 13 line: we reasonably worship Him, having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third.
Marcion teaching his disciples to believe in some other god greater than the Creator.
Irenaeus preserves a line of Justin's lost book against Marcion: I would not have believed the Lord Himself, if He had announced any other than He who is our framer, maker, and nourisher.
Tatian: Crescens endeavoured to inflict on Justin, and indeed on me, the punishment of death.
items.source: Tatian, Address to the Greeks, chapter 19

items.text: McGiffert on Crescens: we have his portrait only from the pen of his bitterest enemies; and on Eusebius's proof: whether his plotting was successful is not stated.
items.source: McGiffert, note 1172 to Eusebius, Church History 4.16

items.text: At the trial: Hierax, Christ is our true father, and faith in Him is our mother; Justin, No right-thinking person falls away from piety to impiety.
items.source: The Martyrdom of Justin, chapters 3 and 4

items.text: The hemlock story: the translator calls it an absurd addition; the editor says it seems to have originated among the Greeks, who naturally gave this turn to the sufferings of a philosopher.

checker_2026_09_25.summary: Every claim on pages/justin-martyr.json checked against the fetched primary texts, the churches' calendars and the Commons licence tags. Fixes listed here; the page and quotes file were corrected to match.
fixes: Shopping for a philosophy: the Pythagorean dismissed him for not knowing 'music, astronomy, and geometry' (Dialogue 2), not geometry alone.

The old man: 'had already shaken him' replaced by Second Apology 12's own sense: while still a Platonist he saw Christians fearless of death and 'perceived that it was impossible that they could be living in wickedness'.
Trypho 'held him by the cloak': the text says 'taking hold of my garment' (Dialogue 9).

Teacher: he 'lived' above Martinus (Martyrdom 2); 'taught from rooms' was a retelling. Role line now 'At his home in Rome'. Irenaeus says Tatian was 'a hearer of Justin's', not that he 'came' to the Rome lodging.
Letter to the emperor: 'to show there was nothing to hide' is not Justin's reason; First Apology 61 says 'lest, if we omit this, we seem to be unfair'.
Crescens: 'in public debate' is Eusebius's (4.16, 'frequently refuted him in public discussions'), not Justin's; cite added, 'in public' dropped from the Justin-cited trait.
Second Apology 13 context: 'Christians have the whole' is not in chapter 13; replaced by 'each man spoke well in proportion to the share he had of the spermatic word'.
Martyrdom: Rusticus told Justin (not all of them) to obey the gods; the companions include a woman (Charito), so 'each said that he was a Christian' became 'they were Christians'.
Last words note: footnote 2647 says Lord Hailes followed 'the common Latin version', not 'the Greek can also be read'.

Sunday: 'the earliest full account' had no source; the Catholic Encyclopedia's 'richness of detail unique for that age' kept. Baptism is 'in the name of God, the Father... and of our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit'. 'Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and others still read it in their own ways' (our voice, unsourced) replaced by the Catholic Encyclopedia's 'with a wonderful clearness' beside the translators' note.
Thousand years: Dialogue 80 says 'a thousand years in Jerusalem, which will then be built'; 'reign' is not in the text.
The Jews: the text says 'you have slain the Just One, and His prophets before Him'; prophets added.
Devil and war: the Goodreads lines closely paraphrase First Apology 39, which says 'refrain from making war', not 'refuse'.

Numbers: chip 'Years after Christ' misread ch. 46 ('Christ was born one hundred and fifty years ago'); now 'Years since Christ's birth'. 'Manuscripts 1' contradicted its own line (two manuscripts exist); now 'Manuscripts we rely on' (CE: 'our sole authority').
Saint section: 'honoured as a martyr from the start' replaced by McGiffert's point that Irenaeus mentions the martyrdom 'casually, as a fact well known'.

Fresco credit: Commons gives 'Theophanes the Cretan and his son Symeon'. Licence PD-Art / PD-old-100 checked; 767x1181 is the largest version on Commons. Thevet engraving: PD-Art / PD-old-auto-1923, 839x1013, matches.
